body.text: Morocco is among the last remaining democratic monarchies in the world; this feature is also one of Morocco’s most innovative aspects. King Mohammed VI came to the throne in 1999 and, ever since, has proven to be a leader in social, legal, and infrastructural reforms alongside his constitutional reforms of 2011. Under his leadership, Morocco has been transforming into a modernized, sophisticated economy, one now increasingly taking its place as a leader in African investment, manufacturing, technology, and energy, while strengthening its place as a bridge between the EU, Africa and Asia.

The economic and industrial development now taking shape across Morocco comes on the heels of socioeconomic transition from a primarily agricultural society to a middle-class industrialized one. Morocco has, for example, become a leading auto supplier and global producer of phosphates, primarily for fertilizer, witnessing a boom in GDP growth from $46.3 billion in 1999 to over $125 billion by 2025. As part of the changes, foreign investors have moved direct investments into the nation as well, preparing the way for hosting the 2030 World Cup, for critical minerals diversification, and for North Africa’s security needs.

This month, King Mohammed VI announced a new iteration of his development plan for the Kingdom, the Defense Industry Facilitation and Acceleration Agency. The agency will be dedicated to mobilizing private investment for defense and for developing advanced technologies like drones, autonomous systems, cyberdefense, and artificial intelligence. Morocco also announced that 40 percent of the equipment needs of its military would come from domestic production by 2035.

The amplification of Morocco’s industrial sector matters significantly to its neighbor, Europe, and the many African countries that rely on Morocco as a supplier and trade facilitator. Ali Seddiki, the head of Morocco’s investment and export promotion agency, already announced that 65% of its revenue is expected to come from exports. The royal strategy, named the ‘Morocco Offer’ is an ambitious roadmap to build a national defense and security industrial base for Morocco, but it also comes as American, Asian, and European businesses have become more involved in the domestic Moroccan economy. In fact, from 2024 to 2025, Morocco saw a 91 percent increase in foreign direct investment in its economy.

King Mohammed VI’s plan, and his consistency in delivering economic growth, forecasts another step in Morocco’s standing as a leading African country. By 2035, the country may look much different than it does now, and with the addition of heightened levels of defense spending, an additional security sector could expand across Northern Africa. Through the Morocco Offer, the nation plans to create around 50,000 direct and indirect jobs and create new industrial defense zones in Benguerir and Benslimane using a 4-billion-dirham contribution from the Hassan II Fund for Economic and Social Development.

Since King Mohammed VI took the throne, his leadership and reformation have carried the nation into a position of leadership for Africa and for the region. In the midst of social reforms, the King has maintained a steady vision of economic reinvigoration through trade, onshoring manufacturing, and attracting international investment. In so doing, Morocco has become a clear competitor to East Asian made goods, offering an attractive choice for businesses seeking to diversify their supply chains.

For a country like the United States, which has made diversification a core concern under the Trump administration, Morocco’s position in Africa, near Europe, and its economic independence from China make it a prime candidate for American investment. King Mohammed VI’s strategy subtly acknowledges this international need for diversification, and the new focus placed on building a defense industry shows that Morocco could offer both quality weapons systems and the ability to replenish them at scale.

Morocco already offers a long slew of strengths for international market competitiveness, with impacts that extend all the way to East Asia. From political continuity, established relationships with Western economies, proximity to European markets, access to African markets, and a growing record of attracting international manufacturing investment, Morocco presents a compelling case. Its existing automotive and aerospace industries further provide a foundation for advancing specialized production. The strategy is poised to incentivize American defense companies to look to nearshore their supply chains across the Atlantic, particularly when looking at the impending threat from China.

King Mohammed VI’s strategy is not new; it follows a top-down centrally planned industrial policy, paired with careful reforms. These are tied to a clear national vision, and the King has positioned Morocco as a politically stable manufacturing hub, growing regional actor, and independent player in the growth of global supply chains. Morocco has made itself known as open to investment capital without depending on any single partner, and is among the few African countries operating without the constraints of Chinese influence. And this strategic step into the defense sector will move Morocco from simply supplying foreign markets to building a sovereign industrial base. The strategy is one that can supply its own military, serve as a regional security anchor, and export to partners across the Atlantic.

The next decade of Moroccan development will demand close attention from American policymakers, who continue, in bipartisan efforts, to decouple from Chinese-led supply chains. Morocco is a major non-NATO ally and is the only African country to have a free trade agreement with the United States. As the Morocco Offer seeks to deliver on its 2035 targets, the United States will continue to have a strong Atlantic partner for nearshoring critical defense supply chains. Hesitation on the part of US policymakers, however, may leave Morocco open to Asian investors likewise eager to move into North Africa.
